posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
It is insane what they did to pull that landing off.  I was obsessed with being an astronaut when I was in Kindergarten, knew about 20 constellations and could tell you shat shuttle was in space and their primary mission on any day.  I would get excited sitting in school knowing while I st there a shuttle was taking off or landing.

1986 was a rough year.  All I wanted for my Birthday was a telescope to see Haley's Comet with.  Then 3 days before my 7th birthday I watched the Challenger break up on TV.  Less than 2 weeks later the light pollution was too much for me and my little telescope to see the comet.

I was depressed at 7 years old.  I stopped caring about the math and science I was years ahead in, I found other things and never went back.

My daughter is going to turn 7 this February.  She has seen live feeds of Astronauts on a space station, and there has been a Mars landing and now a Comet.

A whole new generation connecting to the stars, it is a beautiful thing.

posts.name: arenson9
posts.cooked:
Craig:

It's funny. I was three when this happened. The Challenger explosion is one of my few memories from that time.

The Challenger explosion, along with the fall of the Berlin Wall and 9/11, is one of the few world events where I remember precisely where I was when I learned of it. 

I was 15. We had moved to Hong Kong just weeks before. I was going to a private school for the first time, and a Christian one at that – somewhat alarming, since I'm Jewish. It wasn't a particularly religious school as Christian schools go, seeing as how it was the only American school in Hong Kong and thus serving a quite diverse population, but there were required religion classes, including at least one bible study class. 

So, there I was in "What is religion?", surrounded by kids I hardly knew, living in a foreign country, when an announcement came over the PA that the shuttle had exploded. It was incredibly shocking. I think we had a TV wheeled in to see the newscasts and see the explosion. It seemed unbelievable. Before then my impression of the shuttle program was that it was boring. They seemed safe and routine. They did mission after mission, flew up into space, orbitted around a bit, then came home. I vaguely thought we were behind in our space program. What had we done lately? Why couldn't we go further out in the solar system?

posts.name: grysqrl
posts.cooked: I was six. I remember that they rolled a TV on one of those big carts into the classroom so that we could watch the launch. When things went south, it took us a little bit to understand that it wasn't supposed to happen. I think we just took our cues from the teachers to be sufficiently horrified until it really sunk in.

posts.name: Craig
posts.cooked: Yeah, it's interesting. There were a lot of kids in school that saw this, which is why it sticks In so many brains. Teachers were excited about Christa McAuliffe being onboard, so they wanted students to see. Sadly, that meant a lot of people saw horror instead.

It's really cool that the thing landed okay, even if it apparently "bounced" twice before managing to land properly :D. I haven't seen any of the pics yet, though.
